title: What should you do while the interviewer reads you the case?
description: Everything later links back to the goal you write down now. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: While the interviewer reads you the case, write the client's goal at the top of your page, note the key facts in shorthand, turn the numbers into the size of the problem, and mark anything you do not understand so you can ask about it when they finish. Do not interrupt and do not fake understanding. How you listen in this first minute decides how easy the rest of the case will be.
body:
Stage 1 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why this stage matters

Everything later in the case links back to the goal you write down now. If you miss that the client wants "$10M of profit within two years" and hear only "grow profit", your structure, your maths and your recommendation will all be aimed slightly off target. Assume you will hear the prompt only once.

What to do while you listen

Write the goal first, in a box

Put the client's objective at the top of the page, with its number and deadline: "Restore margin to 12% within a year." This box is the anchor for every answer you give. Glance at it before you speak at each stage.

Note facts in shorthand

Below the goal, write the facts from the prompt in short bullets: who the client is, what has changed, and any numbers. McKinsey's own sample cases tell candidates simply to "take notes of the numbers". Use abbreviations you will recognise later (Rev, Cost, Cust, Mkt) and always attach units: "$10M", not "10". On a video call, Bain's guidance is to let your interviewer know when you are taking notes. It also stops a quiet pause looking like a frozen screen.

Turn numbers into the size of the problem

A small conversion as you write saves time later. Suppose the prompt says a bakery chain's operating margin fell from 12% to 8% while revenue stayed at $10M. Your notes might read:

Goal: restore margin. Rev $10M flat. Margin 12% → 8%. Profit $1.2M → $0.8M = −$400k.

Now you know the scale before drawing any framework: $10M × 12% = $1.2M, $10M × 8% = $0.8M, so about $400k of operating profit has gone. That figure will matter when you judge whether a fix is big enough.

Keep facts apart from guesses

Mark the numbers the interviewer gives you (a tick or a "G" works) and keep any estimate of your own clearly labelled. Five minutes later it is easy to treat your own early guess as data.

Flag what you do not understand

If a word or number is unclear, write a question mark next to it and ask as soon as the interviewer finishes. Interrupting mid-sentence is awkward; staying quiet and building on a misunderstanding is worse.

Notice early clues

Some facts point to the answer the moment you hear them. "Revenue fell while volume held" means price or mix has changed. Circle facts like these. You can mention one briefly in your recap, which shows commercial instinct and gives you a hypothesis to test.

What to say

You will say very little at this stage, which is the point. When the interviewer finishes, these lines cover most situations:

"Thank you, that's an interesting problem. Before I recap, one quick check: when you said contribution, did you mean contribution per unit?"
"Interesting that revenue fell while volume held. That points to price or mix, so I may want to come back to it."

Then move straight to your recap.

Common mistakes

  • Nodding along when you do not understand. You get lost ten minutes later, and recovering costs far more than one question now.
  • Writing everything down. You are not taking minutes. Capture the goal, the changes and the numbers.
  • Numbers without units. "4.5" could be revenue, margin or millions of customers. Write "$4.5M a year".
  • Starting to structure while the interviewer is still talking. You will miss the one fact that changes everything, which often comes last.
  • No goal box. Without it, it is easy to answer a slightly different question at the end. See how to lay out your notes.

Practise the moment

Read the situation and say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. The interviewer has just finished reading the prompt. What do you do first?

Show a strong answer

Check the goal box is complete, with a number and a deadline if they were given, then say: "Thank you, that's an interesting problem." Then recap.

Why it works: A calm opening buys you a second, and checking the goal first means your recap will include it.

2. Mid-prompt, the interviewer says "the client's contribution has fallen" and you are not sure what they mean by contribution.

Show a strong answer

Mark it with a question mark, let them finish, then: "Before I recap, one quick check: when you said contribution, did you mean contribution margin per unit?"

Why it works: Asking at the end of the prompt is polite, and far cheaper than building on a misunderstanding.

3. You hear: "Volumes are stable, but revenue is down 8%." React out loud.

Show a strong answer

"Interesting that revenue fell while volume held. That points to price or mix, so I may want to come back to that."

Why it works: If volume is unchanged, revenue can only fall through a lower average price per unit, from discounts or a shift to cheaper products.

4. The prompt says a hotel's revenue is $50M and occupancy fell from 80% to 70%. What do you write?

Show a strong answer

"Rev $50M. Occ 80% → 70% (−10 pts, so 12.5% fewer rooms sold)." Then ask whether the $50M is before or after the fall.

Why it works: A 10-point fall from 80% is a 12.5% drop in rooms sold (10 ÷ 80), not 10%. Getting this right now avoids a wrong number later.

Where to practise next

Practise listening with a partner reading you prompts from the casebook; interviewer mode shows them what to read aloud. Drill the lines with the flashcards on the perfect casing page, and read how to open a case in the first two minutes to see how listening, recap and clarifying questions fit together.
